vignette:
He is a 68-year-old African man who comes to understand his life in two parts: before the illness and after it. For most of his adult life, he has moved through the world as a policy analyst, a man known for careful thought, measured language, and the habit of preparing for contingencies. He takes pride in being calm under pressure. Even after his wife dies and he begins living alone, he keeps to routines that make the days feel orderly: coffee early, news in the morning, papers spread across the dining table, notes stacked neatly in his briefcase. He tells himself that structure is what keeps a person steady.

That certainty changes when he becomes seriously ill. At first, he dismisses the weakness in his body as fatigue or stress. He has always pushed through discomfort, and he does so now, reasoning that he cannot afford to be distracted. But the symptoms intensify in a way that no amount of discipline can master. He is admitted to the hospital, and the experience quickly becomes one of helplessness. Machines surround him, alarms sound in the night, and people speak in clipped, urgent phrases that he cannot always follow. He remembers trying to make sense of the expressions on the nurses’ faces, looking for reassurance and finding only caution. The fear is not abstract; it is rooted in the sudden certainty that his body is failing and that he may die before he can understand what is happening.

In the weeks that follow, his life narrows to rooms, test results, and the rhythm of waiting. He becomes preoccupied with small signs in his body, studying each ache or flutter as if it might announce another crisis. Sleep becomes broken and untrustworthy. He lies awake listening to his own breathing, startled by every change in pace, convinced that the night is when the worst will happen. Sometimes he wakes with the same jolt he felt in the hospital, drenched in sweat and trying to orient himself to the room around him. In those moments, he is no longer an experienced professional or a widower managing his household alone; he is a frightened man lying still and listening for danger.

He survives, but survival does not restore the ease he expected. Instead, he returns home carrying an invisible vigilance. He keeps checking his pulse, his medication, the color of his skin, the steadiness of his strength. He avoids reading about illness, because even a familiar phrase can send his mind back to the hospital bed. Medical appointments feel unbearable. He can sit in the waiting room with a composed face, but inside he is bracing for bad news, scanning every change in tone from staff, every pause before a doctor speaks. He finds himself replaying the illness over and over, especially at night, not in a clear narrative but in fragments: the smell of antiseptic, the sound of the monitor, the helplessness of being dependent on strangers to tell him whether he will live.

Since his wife’s death, he has already known loneliness, but the illness gives it a different weight. He misses her practical presence most in the moments when he feels frightened and has no one to reach for. He does not always say this aloud, but there is a grief in him that seems to have thickened. He becomes more withdrawn, less willing to answer calls, less interested in the discussions he once enjoyed at work. As a policy analyst, he still reads reports and drafts recommendations, but now he struggles to concentrate for long stretches. His mind drifts to his body, to mortality, to the possibility that another sudden change is coming. He catches himself rereading the same paragraph without taking it in. Meetings that once felt stimulating now leave him tired and irritable.

He notices that he is not only afraid of dying; he is afraid of being caught unprepared. The illness has shaken his faith in his own ability to manage life through reason and discipline. He is embarrassed by how quickly fear rises in him, and he often tries to hide it behind composure. Yet in quiet moments, when the house is still, he feels the old terror returning in his chest, and he sits very still until it passes. His days are organized, but narrowly, as though he is moving around an open wound. Even now, he speaks with the dignity and restraint that have long defined him, but beneath that steadiness is a man who has been changed by an experience of bodily betrayal and who remains watchful, as if danger could return at any moment.
